status: DRAFT - sequences are plausible designs, not validated recommendations. Confirm with UNR Extension (Churchill County) before presenting as evidence-supported.
month_convention: 1-12 calendar months; entries that cross a year boundary use harvest_year greater than year

rotations.name: Current rotation (baseline: alfalfa stand)
rotations.purpose: Represents the regional norm: alfalfa dominates Nevada irrigated acreage and is the main crop in Churchill County.
rotations.justification: A multi-year alfalfa stand gives near-continuous green cover for most of the growing season and is a legume. It is also the most water-demanding option, with local irrigation typically reported at 3.5-4.0 acre-ft per season.
tradeoffs: High water demand during a drought-prone period for the Newlands Project
Already a legume, so the soil-health gap versus other rotations may be small
rotations.evidence_strength: strong for the baseline being typical; moderate for the exact transition-crop sequence

rotations.name: Alternative A: Water-conserving small-grain and pea rotation
rotations.purpose: Lower seasonal water demand than alfalfa or corn by using small grains and a short-season legume.

optional_swap.note: Teff used about 2.9 acre-ft in one 2004 Fallon trial versus 3.5-4.0 for alfalfa; evidence is limited to a single trial year.

rotations.justification: Short-season cereals and field pea finish before late-summer peak demand, so seasonal water use is expected to be lower than alfalfa or corn. Field pea adds a legume without a perennial water commitment.
tradeoffs: Longer bare-soil periods after harvest (July to the next spring) than a perennial stand
Water and N benefits of field pea at Fallon are not well documented
rotations.evidence_strength: moderate (crop water values from FAO-56; limited local data)

rotations.name: Alternative B: Soil-health rotation with legume and winter cover
rotations.purpose: Maximize potential soil-health contributions through cover crops, a legume cash crop and reduced bare soil.

optional_swap.note: Soybean is under trial at the UNR Fallon Research Center; Fallon season length makes maturity uncertain.

rotations.justification: Cover crops reduce bare soil and add organic matter inputs, and legumes fix nitrogen that can reduce fertilizer needs for the following crop. A rye cover tested at the NRCS Fallon center showed excellent winter hardiness and weed suppression.
tradeoffs: Cover crops use water in an arid system; terminating before seed set limits this
Corn silage is water-intensive and may not work every year at Fallon
Hairy vetch showed variable emergence and winter survival (60-100%) in the Fallon study
rotations.evidence_strength: moderate (good local cover crop evidence; limited local N and water-saving evidence)
